analysis.one_liner: Bans broadband internet providers from imposing data caps on customers, with narrow exceptions for congestion management.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban broadband data caps was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in July 2022 and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit home internet providers from capping how much data customers can use before charging overage fees, slowing speeds, or pushing them into pricier plans. Providers could only impose caps if the cap is genuinely tailored to managing network congestion, and the FCC would have to write rules within 270 days defining what counts as a legitimate cap and enforce the ban under the Communications Act. The bill's findings note that broadband networks performed strongly through the pandemic's record usage, evidence that many networks can handle high usage without caps.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that pay overage charges, rent unlimited-data plans, or get throttled after hitting their provider's cap. Rural and low-income households, families with remote work, school, and telehealth needs, and anyone with heavy video, gaming, or smart-home usage would keep full-speed service without watching a usage meter.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars broadband providers from imposing data caps that trigger fees, higher per-unit prices, or reduced speeds unless the cap is tailored primarily to reasonable network management or congestion management [S2].

The bill requires the FCC to write regulations within 270 days of enactment defining what counts as a tailored data cap, and to enforce the ban as part of the Communications Act, so violations carry real legal consequences [S2].

Congress' stated findings in the bill say internet access is essential for work, education, and health care, and that networks' strong performance during COVID-19 demand spikes shows many networks can accommodate much higher usage without caps [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers lose a significant revenue stream: overage fees, per-gigabyte charges, and paid unlimited-data add-ons. Some providers argue caps fund network investment and shift costs to the heaviest users; under the bill, any lost fee revenue would need to come from base pricing or thinner margins.

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges some networks may need congestion-management practices, and by allowing caps 'tailored' to network management, it leaves the FCC to draw the line — which could leave room for providers to keep caps dressed up as congestion tools [S2].

Providers and some network engineers argue usage-based pricing helps fund network capacity and that a ban could concentrate costs on all customers rather than heavy users; the bill does not cap the base price providers can charge instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and widely felt: removing metered billing on a service most households depend on daily. The main cost is that it intervenes in how ISPs price their networks, and its effectiveness depends heavily on how strictly the FCC defines a 'tailored' cap. It does not address the underlying prices providers charge, only the capping practice on top of them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2022 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the bill on July 21, 2022, with Senator Cory Booker, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S3].
The bill never advanced beyond committee referral — no markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, Senator Booker, giving it no evident path to a vote in the Senate [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers keep collecting data-cap overage fees and paid unlimited plans, and no household gets relief from metered internet billing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers, whose caps stay in place

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over broadband policy
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it did not advance in a Senate then split 48 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 50 Republicans [S4].

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable, fiber, and DSL companies)
industries.note: Data caps create fee revenue through overage charges and paid unlimited plans; the bill would eliminate that pricing practice except where caps genuinely manage congestion. Households currently pay extra or get slowed once they hit caps.
Caps and throttling discourage heavy streaming and app usage; removing caps removes a friction between customers and the services they use.
The bill hands the FCC explicit statutory authority to define and enforce limits on data caps, expanding its broadband consumer-protection role.
